title: Appel à la maternité  (Call at the Maternity Ward)

segments.t: At the maternity clinic, Andrea Martel has just given birth to her baby daughter with her partner Colette by her side. When prominent client Fabrice Luchini calls her phone, Andrea answers immediately despite the hospital setting. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Tu n'es pas obligée de répondre.
Je ne veux pas disparaître du jour au lendemain.
Mais si, tu es à la maternité!
Je ne peux pas perdre Fabrice!
Allô Fabrice? Tu vas bien?
Merci, c'est vraiment très gentil.
Écoute, tout se passe super bien.
La petite fille est vraiment magnifique.
Ne t'inquiète pas du tout.
Andréa, s'il te plaît, raccroche maintenant.
Fabrice, je peux te rappeler?
J'ai un imprévu en ce moment.
Merci, pensons enfin à notre bébé.
Let's explore how Andrea balances client demands with new motherhood line by line.
Tu n'es pas obligée de répondre.
'You do not have to answer.' Colette gently tells Andrea to ignore her ringing mobile phone. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past verb form for 'obliged'.
Je ne veux pas disparaître du jour au lendemain.
'I do not want to disappear overnight.' Andrea insists that she must remain available for top talent. Notice the classic French sandwich negation wrapping right around 'want'.
Mais si, tu es à la maternité!
'Oh yes, you are in the maternity ward!' Colette reminds her that she just delivered their daughter. The key noun here means 'maternity clinic!', anchored by its matching French article.
Je ne peux pas perdre Fabrice!
'I cannot afford to lose Fabrice!' Andrea refuses to risk her relationship with star actor Fabrice Luchini. The two-part French negation brackets the verb for 'can' on both sides.
Allô Fabrice? Tu vas bien?

'Hello Fabrice? Are you doing well?' Andrea answers her client with energetic professional cheer. In everyday spoken French, rising intonation on 'are going' at the end is enough to turn the sentence into a question.
Merci, c'est vraiment très gentil.

'Thank you, that is truly very kind.' Andrea warmly receives Fabrice's congratulations on the newborn baby. In spoken French, the little word before 'it is' drops its final vowel and attaches with an apostrophe.
Écoute, tout se passe super bien.

'Listen, everything is going super well.' Andrea assures him that motherhood will not disrupt their work. The short 'self' word sits right in front of the verb for 'listen', turning the action back onto the subject.
La petite fille est vraiment magnifique.
'The little girl is truly magnificent.' Andrea shares a tender description of their newborn infant. The key noun here means 'girl', anchored by its matching French article.
Ne t'inquiète pas du tout.

'Do not worry at all.' Andrea comforts Fabrice about his upcoming movie schedule and costume concerns. The short 'self' word sits right in front of the verb for 'worry', turning the action back onto the subject.
Andréa, s'il te plaît, raccroche maintenant.
'Andrea, please hang up right now.' Colette tries to steer Andrea's attention back to family time. The informal 'you' form around 'pleases' marks a direct, personal relationship.
Fabrice, je peux te rappeler?

'Fabrice, can I call you back?' Andrea finally concedes and prepares to pause the conversation. In everyday spoken French, rising intonation on 'can' at the end is enough to turn the sentence into a question.
J'ai un imprévu en ce moment.
'I have an unexpected situation right now.' Andrea invents an urgent excuse to end the work call. Notice how 'I have' leads directly into the noun meaning 'unexpected event'.
Merci, pensons enfin à notre bébé.

'Thank you, let's finally think about our baby.' Colette welcomes Andrea back into their peaceful hospital room. The verb meaning 'let's think' pairs naturally with the noun for 'baby.' in everyday conversation. Now let's listen to the maternity clinic conversation once more to solidify what you have learned.

That's it for this scene around call at the maternity ward. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'are not' and 'obliged'. You'll catch them now. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
